header: \post{Absence of Evidence Is Evidence of Absence}{Eliezer Yudkowsky}{2007}{https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/mnS2WYLCGJP2kQkRn/absence-of-evidence-is-evidence-of-absence}
notes: \cpara{The post opens with its one real case, borrowed whole from a 1988 textbook, and does not check it (see the fact note in the quotation). After two paragraphs the case is dropped, and the internment itself, ``a most grievous chapter,'' receives no comment of the author's own.}
\cpara{Quotes Dawes on Earl Warren's 1942 testimony that the absence of sabotage by Japanese-Americans was the most ominous sign, as an example of fitting evidence to a conclusion.}

\cfact{Warren was not governor. He was California's Attorney General from 1939 to 1943; he was elected governor on 3 November 1942 and sworn in on 4 January 1943 (California State Library, Governors of California). The post passes the error on without comment. I could not check Dawes's printed text.}
\cpara{Explains the Bayesian rule: evidence shifts probability toward the hypotheses that made it more likely, so what matters is how the likelihoods compare.}
\cpara{Applies it to Warren: a hidden group might delay sabotage, but no sabotage is still more likely if no such group exists.}
\cpara{Defines the symbols: sabotage seen or not seen, a hidden group or none, and the chance of the evidence given each hypothesis.}

\cpara{The formal step against Warren. ``Won't be as large'' follows directly, since without a Fifth Column there is no Fifth Column sabotage. But it concedes less than the post thinks. On Warren's own hypothesis, a Fifth Column holding everything for one coordinated day, the two likelihoods are, by my inference, nearly equal. The absence of sabotage is then almost no evidence either way, the ``very weak'' case of the post's later paragraph. The post does not apply its later paragraph to its opening case.}

\cpara{This paragraph concedes what the slogan in the title's target actually says. The post never quotes or attributes the slogan ``absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.'' Carl Sagan, in \textsc{The Demon-Haunted World}, uses it against the ``appeal to ignorance: the claim that whatever has not been proved false must be true.'' That is a point about proof, which is this paragraph's point. The title fights the slogan by reading ``evidence'' in a sense its users did not intend.}

\cpara{The theorem. ``Always'' is correct but carries a condition, given in the next sentence: ``If \ldots\ P(H | E) > P(H).'' The rule covers only observations that would have raised the probability of H.}

\cpara{The qualification that undoes the title: absence may be ``strong evidence of absence or very weak evidence of absence.'' The title states the rule without it. Here it comes in the second-to-last paragraph.}
\cpara{Argues that a model's strength lies in what it rules out; one that explains every outcome equally well gives no knowledge.}
\cpara{A footnote pointing confused readers to the author's longer explanation of Bayesian updating in a book volume.}
